item.title: New Home Sales Reinforce Last Month's Rebound
item.author: Mortgage News Daily
item.content:encoded: New home sales lost almost no ground in September, effectively reinforcing the healthy rebound seen in August's report. The Census Bureau's New Residential Construction report clocked sales at an annual pace of 676k, down only 0.6% month over month. As seen in the chart below, the broader trend has been sideways for nearly 3 years now. The number of new houses for sale slipped to 476,000 , down 1.0% from August and 2.3% from a year earlier. With inventory edging lower alongside sales, the implied supply eased to 8.4 months , compared with 8.5 months in August and 8.2 months last September. Prices rebounded from August's decline. The median sales price rose to $400,400 , up 3.9% for the month but still 3.9% below September 2025. The average sales price increased 0.4% to $472,800 , leaving it 6.7% below its year-ago level. item.title: Home Price Appreciation Edges Higher in August
item.author: Mortgage News Daily
item.content:encoded: Home price appreciation picked up again in August (as reported this week), but the improvement was minimal. The FHFA House Price Index rose 0.3% from July to August, bringing annual appreciation to 2.4% . July's previously reported monthly gain was revised down from 0.3% to 0.2%. Regional results remained uneven, with annual appreciation ranging from 0.5% in the Mountain division to 4.4% in the East North Central division. Case-Shiller's national index rose 2.1% year over year, up from 1.9% in July. The 10-City Composite gained 3.6% , while the 20-City Composite rose 2.7% . Even with the recent improvement, the inflation-adjusted trend remains negative. Consumer prices rose 3.4% annually in August, well above the 2.1% increase in national home prices. That gap has persisted for more than a year, offering some relief on a relative affordability basis even as elevated home prices and mortgage rates continue to challenge buyers. Case-Shiller's metro-level results continued to show a sharp divide between markets. Chicago led the 20 tracked cities for the sixth consecutive month , with prices up 6.7% year over year. New York followed at 6.2%, and Cleveland gained 4.3%. Seattle remained at the other end of the spectrum, with prices down 2.0% annually, followed by Las Vegas at -1.3% and Denver at -0.8%. item.title: Mortgage Demand Bounces Back, Sort Of
item.author: Mortgage News Daily
item.content:encoded: Mortgage applications finally rebounded as mortgage rates fell for a second straight week. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a 3.4% increase in total application volume for the week ending October 23. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate declined to 7.37% from 7.41%, its lowest level in three weeks. Both purchase and refinance applications moved higher, but just barely, and well below levels from last year. The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index rose 4% for the week, and still 18% below year-ago levels . Refinances increased 3%, offering only a modest rebound from a market still 61% below its level a year earlier. “The decline in rates gave borrowers some relief, with applications rebounding slightly, particularly conventional applications,” said MBA's Joel Kan. He noted that mortgage rates remain more than a percentage point above year-ago levels, while most homeowners have little incentive to refinance. Adjustable-rate mortgages accounted for 11.3% of applications , the highest share in more than a year, as borrowers sought lower monthly payments. item.title: Rethinking Marketing in a Tight Farm Economy
item.author: Farm Journal
item.content:encoded: When Farmers Weigh Whether to Buy Now, Buy Later or Hold Off Entirely, Is Your Marketing Built to Help Them Decide?Farm Journal’s September 2026 Ag Economists Monthly Monitor takes a closer look at fertilizer prices, but the story goes beyond one input. It’s no secret that rising costs, tight margins and economic uncertainty are influencing how producers prioritize spending and make purchasing decisions. While fertilizer is just one piece of the puzzle, it reflects broader financial pressures across agriculture. For ag marketers heading into 2027, the question is: How should these realities shape where brands invest, how they communicate value and what it takes to earn a producer’s business?What Makes the Outlook Difficult? Economists recommend different approaches to fertilizer purchases, while price expectations vary. Brands should be careful about assuming customers will all make decisions at the same time.Pressure extends beyond one input. Fertilizer costs, financing and other operating needs compete for working capital. In a separate June Farm Journal economist report, 50% expected broadly profitable crop margins to be three to five years away.External forces can change the plan. Global production, trade policies and fertilizer input costs may shift the outlook after marketing calendars and farm plans have already been set.The biggest competitor may be the decision not to buy.Five Marketing Decisions to Revisit for 2027For ag marketers, the challenge is not only to win preference over another brand. It is to help customers justify investing at all.*This is a marketing interpretation of the economic findings, not a conclusion measured by the panel.Before You Finalize the Plan, Ask:Are we competing against another brand, a lower-cost option or no purchase at all?What proof would a skeptical customer need to defend the investment?Does our marketing strategy still work if purchasing decisions are delayed by 90 days?When Buying Gets Harder, Marketing Matters MoreA tighter farm economy doesn’t automatically mean marketing should go quiet. It means the marketing that helps customers make difficult decisions may matter more.

item.title: Mortgage Applications Aren't Ready to Rebound Just Yet
item.author: Mortgage News Daily
item.content:encoded: Mortgage applications continued to decline even as mortgage rates finally moved lower. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a 5.3% drop in total application volume for the week ending October 16, despite the first weekly decline in mortgage rates in more than two months. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to 7.41% from 7.50% the previous week. That improvement wasn't enough to revive demand, with both purchase and refinance applications moving lower. The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index fell 7% for the week and was 18% below year-ago levels . Refinances fared somewhat better, declining 2%, though activity remained 59% lower than a year earlier. “Purchase applications fell 18 percent behind last year's pace, as higher rates are pricing buyers out of the market,” said MBA's Joel Kan, who also noted that adjustable-rate mortgages remain an option for qualified borrowers looking for lower rates. ARMs held steady at 10.5% of applications , with rates nearly a full percentage point below the 30-year fixed average. The refinance share of total applications increased to 39.0% from 37.7% the previous week. That shift came despite the decline in refinance volume, reflecting the steeper drop in purchase applications. item.title: Building Permits Hold Steady Despite Slide in Housing Starts
item.author: Mortgage News Daily
item.content:encoded: Residential construction failed to find even footing in September, with housing starts declining and single-family building permits pulling back, while total permits held nearly steady and completions edged higher. This week's Census Bureau data highlights weakness in new construction, particularly on the single-family side, while starts and completions were comparatively stable. Privately owned housing starts fell 5.2% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.221 million , down 7.4% from September 2025. Single-family starts declined 4.6% to 859k , and multi-family came in at 349k . Building permits were more stable, slipping just 0.2% to an annual rate of 1.400 million , although they were 3.0% below the September 2025 pace. Single-family authorizations fell 4.0% to 845k , while multi-family permits rose to 503k . The contrast between total permits and single-family authorizations suggests that the overall pipeline for future construction was relatively steady, even as the single-family segment weakened. Multi-family permits accounted for a larger share of total authorizations in September, though monthly figures can fluctuate considerably in that segment. Housing completions bounced back from last month, and increased 2.2% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.192 million , still 14.0% below the September 2025 rate. Single-family completions slipped 2.4% to 840k , multi-family completions came in at 339k .

item.title: Builder Confidence Hits Lowest Level Since 2012
item.author: Mortgage News Daily
item.content:encoded:
The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) dropped three points to 29 in October--its lowest level in 14 years. As per usual, higher mortgage rates, rising costs, and worsening labor and lot conditions were the driving factors. All three component indices declined, with prospective buyer traffic suffering the steepest drop.
HMI Component September October Change
Current sales conditions 35 33 -2
Sales expectations 37 32 -5
Prospective buyer traffic 23 18 -5
"Buyer traffic has now fallen to its lowest level since April 2012, excluding the initial pandemic shock in April 2020.” said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens. Builders are also facing higher construction loan, material and diesel costs, along with construction delays tied to immigration enforcement activity. Builders have responded by continuing to slash prices. The share reporting price cuts climbed to 43% in October, the highest level during the 2020-2026 period. The average reduction remained at 6% for the seventh consecutive month. Sales incentives were reported by 65% of builders, marking the 19th straight month that at least 60% have offered them.
